nameStory: The hummingbird clearwing earned its name from its uncanny resemblance to a tiny hummingbird as it hovers at flowers, wings beating so fast they blur into transparency. The 'clearwing' part refers to its transparent wings that lose their scales shortly after the moth emerges, creating see-through panels that catch the light like tiny windows.
description: The hummingbird clearwing is a day-flying moth that looks remarkably like a small hummingbird or large bumblebee. Its body is olive green and burgundy on top with a white or yellow and burgundy belly, while its wings are mostly transparent with reddish-brown borders. This fascinating moth hovers at flowers just like a hummingbird, beating its wings rapidly to collect nectar. It's about the size of a large bumblebee, making it one of the more noticeable moths you'll encounter in New England gardens.

idTips.label: Transparent wings
idTips.description: Wings are mostly clear like glass with reddish-brown borders - you can see right through them as the moth hovers

idTips.label: Light-colored legs
idTips.description: Legs are pale yellow or whitish, contrasting with the darker body - easily visible as it feeds at flowers

idTips.label: Hovering flight
idTips.description: Hovers motionless at flowers with wings beating so fast they're nearly invisible, creating a soft humming sound

idTips.label: Olive and burgundy body
idTips.description: Back is olive green mixed with deep burgundy, while the belly is white or yellow with burgundy patches

idTips.label: Lack of stripes underneath
idTips.description: Belly is solid colored without the black stripes that mark its close relative, the snowberry clearwing

idTips.label: Daytime activity
idTips.description: Active during bright daylight hours, especially mid-morning to afternoon when flowers are fully open

habitat: Look for hummingbird clearwings in sunny gardens, meadows, and woodland edges throughout New England where nectar-rich flowers bloom. They're especially common around residential areas with flower gardens, parks, and anywhere native honeysuckle or cultivated flowering plants provide abundant nectar sources. These moths prefer open or semi-open areas with good sun exposure rather than deep forest interiors.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late May and early June, often seen visiting lilac, wild columbine, and other early summer flowers in gardens and woodland edges.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months when adults are most abundant at flowers like bee balm, phlox, and honeysuckle. This is the best time to spot them hovering at garden flowers.
seasonality.fall: A second generation appears in late summer through early fall in southern New England, visiting late-blooming flowers like jewelweed and wild bergamot.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent; the species overwinters as pupae in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to emerge as the next generation of moths.

funFact: This moth is such a convincing hummingbird mimic that it can fool experienced birdwatchers at first glance - but unlike real hummingbirds, it has antennae and will land on flowers to rest between feeding sessions!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for an actual hummingbird or large bumblebee due to its hovering behavior and size. Unlike hummingbirds, it has antennae and fuzzy moth body parts rather than feathers, and unlike bees, its wings are transparent rather than solid-colored. Memory trick: 'Clear wings, it's the moth that sings' (referring to its humming flight sound).
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'hummingbird' moth, this species is actually more closely related to the large sphinx moths that come to porch lights at night. The daytime activity and hummingbird-like appearance represent an evolutionary strategy called Batesian mimicry, where harmless species benefit by resembling something else.
compareHints: The hummingbird clearwing differs from its close relative, the snowberry clearwing, by having light-colored legs and a solid-colored belly without black stripes. While both have transparent wings and similar hovering behavior, the snowberry clearwing has darker legs and distinctive black stripes across its yellow underside. The hummingbird clearwing also tends to be slightly larger and more olive-green on top.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The snowberry clearwing is very similar to its cousin the hummingbird clearwing, but has yellow bands on its legs while the hummingbird clearwing has black legs.
